deep.reconstruction:
The page holds raw observing notes and their reduction for an astronomical determination, almost certainly of longitude by lunar distances. The next page carries the follow-up: 'Pariser Zeit', 'Wahre Zeit', declination, horizontal parallax 'Hor P.', and the solution of the spherical triangle with sides D, a, b, half-sum S and angles A, B. There is no pure mathematics on the page.

(1) Sextant index error and solar diameter (top right). Two readings of the Sun's diameter were taken, one off the arc (-31'15") and one on the arc (+33'50").
- Half their difference is the index error: (33'50" - 31'15")/2 = 1'17.5". Gauss writes 1'17,5.
- Half their sum is the apparent solar diameter: (31'15" + 33'50")/2 = 32'32.5". Gauss writes 32'32".
- A diameter this large means the Sun was near perihelion, i.e. a winter observation.

(2) 'Horizont' (top). These are artificial-horizon (double) altitudes against clock times.
- The pairs are 54'33" -> 53°35'5", 55'59" -> 53°37'15", 56'58" -> 53°38'30".
- The small group 33'8", 30'0", 31'38", '30 5' consists of auxiliary diameter or index readings.

(3) Left block of altitudes versus times. The entries 54°18'45" @42'19", 54°18'50" @43'38" and 54°50'20" @45'2" are one set. The entries 53°34'20" @52'4", 53°3'30" @53'30", 53°36'52" @55'35" and 53°6'30" @57'0" are another.
- In the second set the readings alternate by about 30'50" and 30'22". These are upper-limb and lower-limb observations differing by roughly one solar diameter.
- These altitudes serve to find local time and the altitudes used in clearing the distance.

(4) 'Mural 2h 48' 33"'. This is a clock time of a transit with the mural quadrant (clock correction). The column 43 18.5, 13.25, 14.50, 17.00, 19.00 lists further clock readings.

(5) Small computations in the middle: 198/36, 11/60, '0s 11°50'' (a longitude in signs and degrees), 12.606, 12.62, 15.78, and 15.89 - 2.44 = 13.4[5], next to a Moon symbol. These are probably semidiameter or parallax quantities for the Moon. They are too fragmentary to reconstruct with certainty.

(6) Main reduction: the lunar distance series (bottom left). The pairs are clock time (minutes:seconds after some hour) and the observed distance 76°35'25" + increments:
- 0:41 -> 35'25"; 7:28 -> 37'50"; 10:33 -> 39'3"; 12:10 -> 39'40"; 13:39 -> 40'13"
- 15:17 -> 40'47"; 17:16 -> 41'42"; 33:40 -> 47'40".

Rate of change of the distance. From the first to the seventh observation, Δt = 17:16 - 0:41 = 995 s and Δd = 41'42" - 35'25" = 377". Gauss writes 377/995" = 0"379 per second. Over the whole series, 1979 s and 735" appear among the right-margin figures, giving 735/1979 = 0.3714. The entries 0"354 and 3/8 + 1/96 = 37/96 ≈ 0.385 look like trial rates or convenient multipliers.

(7) Reduction to a common epoch (right column). Each of the six observations from 7:28 to 17:16 is reduced to the epoch 5h 15' 0" (written in the middle of the page) via d(T) = d_i + 0.379·(T - t_i). My recomputation:
- 7:28: 37'50" + 0.379·452 s = 40'41.3"
- 10:33: 39'3" + 0.379·267 = 40'44.2"
- 12:10: 39'40" + 0.379·170 = 40'44.4"
- 13:39: 40'13" + 0.379·81 = 40'43.7"
- 15:17: 40'47" - 0.379·17 = 40'40.6"
- 17:16: 41'42" - 0.379·136 = 40'50.5"

These match Gauss's column 40 41, 40 44, 40 44, 40 43, 40 41, 40 50 exactly. Their mean is (41+44+44+43+41+50)/6 = 43.8", which Gauss rounds to 40'44". The result is a mean observed distance of 76°40'44" at 5h15m0s (clock).

The 0:41 and 33:40 observations are used only for the rate, not in the mean. The scattered small products in the right margin (87, 261, 197, 591, 316, 948, 1979, 1960, ...) are side multiplications for these reductions; several are ×3 multiples, e.g. 87·3 = 261 and 197·3 = 591.

(8) Context. The next page applies index error, semidiameters (+15'53.1", +15'31.5"), refraction and parallax to obtain the true distance 77°8'47". It then compares with tabulated distances to get Paris time, i.e. the longitude.
errors: 15.89 - 2.44 = 13.45, but the page appears to read 13.41. This is either a slip or a misreading of one of the digits; the image is faint.

The rates 0.379"/s (first 995 s) and 0.3714"/s (whole 1979 s series) differ noticeably. Gauss uses 0.379 for the reduction, which fits the six reduced observations well. This is not an error, but it shows the rate is not constant over the full interval (Moon's motion plus changing parallax and refraction).

results.what: Index error and apparent solar diameter from on-arc and off-arc sextant readings (half difference and half sum).
results.modern_name: Sextant index correction by solar diameter

results.what: Linear reduction of a series of lunar-distance readings to a common epoch using the observed rate (0.379"/s), followed by the mean.
results.modern_name: Reduction of observations to a mean epoch / linear interpolation
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice of the lunar-distance method (Maskelyne, Nautical Almanac, 1767 onward)

results.what: Overall purpose: longitude determination by lunar distance (completed on the next page with Paris time).
results.usually_credited_to: Werner (1514) for the idea; Mayer and Maskelyne for the practical method

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine record of sextant and mural observations and their arithmetic reduction for a lunar-distance longitude. Gauss's activity as a practical astronomer is well documented, and nothing here is mathematically non-standard.

checkable.asserts: Half sum of on/off readings = 32'32.5" (solar diameter)
The interval and the distance change behind 377/995

transcription_corrections: '12606' should read '12.606' (decimal point; written above 12.62 and 15.78).
The 'D' with '11' is a Moon symbol (☽).
'5^h 15° 0"' is a time, 5h 15' 0" (minutes, not degrees). It is the epoch to which the distance series is reduced.
'73 [?]' in the right margin is probably 735, written over or near 2037; '1979' and '735' are the whole-series interval and distance change.
In the 33:40 line the struck '40' is replaced; the distance reads 47'40".
'D [?]' near 13 41 is the Moon sign; the subtraction is 15.89 - 2.44.
The top-right entries read 53°35'5", [53°]37'15", [53°]38'30" (altitudes) against clock times 54'33", 55'59", 56'58".
